rationale: PINS taint SINKS as receiver-based, the family contract (java: stmt.executeQuery; python: cursor.execute — never a bare execute()). Pre-fix the rules matched a bare name or a bare LEAF, so `re.exec(input)` (RegExp.prototype.exec), a project-local `execute(q)` and `this.spawn(cmd)` were all reported as command_injection / sql_injection. This is not a payload-only defect: parallel-indexer multiplies every taint SOURCE by every SINK in a symbol into brain_taint_flow and bb_security reports that table, so one `req.body` read beside a `.exec()` call manufactured a persisted command-injection finding. The `danger` entry is the shape that made it a security finding: same user input, but a REAL child_process sink, which must still flow. TRUE-POSITIVE retention is pinned as carefully as the fix: a bare `exec(cmd)` is a sink only because THIS file imports child_process (the AST evidence, gathered in the same single walk the React gate already paid for), the db-shaped member call, and res/fs rules which were already receiver-shaped and are untouched. This fixture also required adding the expectTaintSinks GATE itself — the sink payload had no gate at all before this wave, which is why the false positive was never checkable.

expectTaintSinks.note: TRUE POSITIVE, and the hard one: a BARE exec-family name. It qualifies only because this file imports node:child_process — the signal the rule reads off the AST, replacing the pre-fix 'any bare exec is a shell' shortcut.
TRUE POSITIVE: receiver-based database sink, unchanged by the fix
THE POINT OF THE FIX: identical user input, but a real sink — the flow must still be reportable. The false positives were not 'too few findings', they were findings attached to the wrong code.
FALSE POSITIVE 1: RegExp.prototype.exec is not a shell. Pre-fix this symbol carried a command_injection sink.
FALSE POSITIVE 2: the project's own execute().
FALSE POSITIVE 3: the project's own spawn method — the leaf matched, the receiver did not.
